source: Desimone and Duncan (1995) Neural mechanisms of selective visual attention
finding: Founding statement of biased competition. Objects in view compete for neural representation. A top-down bias, set by the held target template, favours cells that code the relevant object. The source page returned 403, so this line rests on the Europe PMC record and on how later papers cite it.
numbers: Record only. About 4,866 citations in Europe PMC.
limits: Not read in full this session. Exact predictions come from secondary description (Soto and Humphreys 2008; Sasin and Nieuwenstein 2016).
agent_relevance: Held content is a bias signal. It does not choose, it tilts a competition. Any item matching a held lesson gets a head start, useful or not.

source: Chelazzi, Miller, Duncan, Desimone (1993) A neural basis for visual search in inferior temporal cortex
finding: Monkeys held a picture cue in memory, then saw 2 to 5 choice pictures. Cue-selective inferotemporal cells kept firing through the delay. About 90 to 120 ms before the saccade to the target, responses to non-targets were suppressed and the target dominated the cell response.
numbers: Choice array of 2-5 pictures; suppression of non-targets 90-120 ms before the eye movement.
limits: Abstract only. Single-cell recordings in few monkeys. The cue was always the target (no matching distractor).
agent_relevance: Neural source of the idea that memory sets up a template and selection suppresses rivals. Does not show the cost when the match is a distractor.

source: Chelazzi, Duncan, Miller, Desimone (1998) Responses of neurons in inferior temporal cortex during memory-guided visual search
finding: Cells showed higher delay activity after a good cue than a poor cue, and higher baseline if the animal expected the good cue. When the array appeared, responses first ignored which item was target, then within 150 to 200 ms were set by the target. If the target was the good stimulus, the response became equal to the response to it alone.
numbers: Array of 2-5 items; target-determined response within 150-200 ms of array onset.
limits: Abstract only. Macaque IT, cue always target.
agent_relevance: Gives a time course: first the bias is a head start, later rivals are suppressed. A model with a late check could mimic this.

source: Downing (2000) Interactions between visual working memory and selective attention
finding: First behavioural demonstration. A sample object held in working memory pulled attention to a matching object shown beside a novel one, measured with a probe task. A matched task with no memory requirement showed the opposite pattern.
numbers: Effect generalised across object type, probe task and memory task (exact ms not read).
limits: Abstract only. Single held item. Soto and Humphreys (2008) note Downing and Dodds (2004) used articulatory suppression and 2 to 3 items and found no pull.
agent_relevance: Held content matters when it is held. Merely seeing something did not give the pull. A lesson must be active in context to bias.

source: Soto, Heinke, Humphreys, Blanco (2005) Early, involuntary top-down guidance of attention from working memory
finding: Four experiments. Observers found a tilted line among vertical lines, each inside a coloured shape. A held shape matching the shape around the target sped search. A held shape matching a distractor slowed search. The effect touched the shortest RTs and the first saccade. It happened even when the held item was never the target (Exp 4), and not when the cue did not need to be held.
numbers: Soto and Humphreys (2008, p.924) summarise: invalid slower, valid faster, against a neutral baseline. Exact ms not in the abstract.
limits: Abstract plus second-hand description. PDF link returned 404. Single held item, short 188 ms gap.
agent_relevance: Core finding behind our fixation worry: a held item biases selection even when it is always wrong for the task.

source: Soto and Humphreys (2008) Stressing the mind: cognitive load and articulatory suppression on attentional guidance from working memory, Exp 1
finding: Exp 1 (one held item, three gaps of 188, 504, 1008 ms): search was slower when the held item reappeared on a distractor. The cost did not shrink as the gap grew, and did not depend on target saliency.
numbers: N=10. Invalid 1,209 ms vs neutral 1,146 ms, F(1,9)=11.23, p=.008. Low-saliency targets 1,378 vs high 977 ms. Validity x ISI F(2,18)=0.14, p=.86. Fastest responses 780 vs 739 ms, F(1,9)=9.25, p=.014. Search error about 1%.
limits: Small N=10. Median RT.
agent_relevance: The pull is not a short-lived priming trace. It lasts over the first second after encoding.
quote: Performance was slower on invalid trials than on neutral trials

source: Soto and Humphreys (2008) Exp 2: articulatory suppression with one held item
finding: With two spoken digits repeated during the memory display (to block verbal recoding), the cost of a matching distractor remained, but it was clearer at the longest gap. The guidance is not only verbal.
numbers: N=15. Invalid 1,049 vs neutral 991 ms, F(1,14)=16.24, p=.001. Validity x ISI F(2,28)=4.92, p=.025. Fastest-end validity effects (5th, 10th percentile) not reliable, F<1.
limits: The earliest (fast-response) part of the effect was lost under suppression; only the slower part stayed.
agent_relevance: Blocking the verbal route weakens the earliest bias but does not remove it. For an LLM everything is verbal, so there is no separate route to block.

source: Soto and Humphreys (2008) Exp 3: two held items, no suppression
finding: Raising memory load from one to two items did not remove the pull of a matching distractor. Either of the two held objects could return on a distractor.
numbers: N=14. Invalid 1,101 vs neutral 1,015 ms, F(1,13)=11.5, p=.005. Memory accuracy about 76%. Validity effect did not differ from Exp 1, F(1,22)=1.04.
limits: Only low-saliency targets used.
agent_relevance: More held items did not by itself switch the pull off. This is the first half of the conflict with load theory.

source: Soto and Humphreys (2008) Exp 4: two held items plus articulatory suppression
finding: With high memory load combined with suppression, the pull of the matching distractor disappeared. The authors conclude that competition for resources in working memory sets the size and time course of the guidance.
numbers: N=14. Invalid 980 vs neutral 954 ms, F(1,13)=3.68, p=.077 (not significant). Exp 3 vs Exp 4 validity x experiment F(1,26)=4.25, p=.049. Exp 2 vs 4 three-way F(2,54)=3.57, p=.038; cost bigger at the longest gap in Exp 2 than Exp 4, t(27)=3.53, p=.001. Memory accuracy about 80%.
limits: Exp 4 effect not significant by itself; cross-experiment interactions are borderline (p=.049, .038). Small samples.
agent_relevance: Pull depends on how much of memory other work uses up. A scaffold that crowds the context may weaken each item's bias rather than strengthen it.

source: Soto and Humphreys (2008) reconciliation of positive and null findings
finding: Names three differences that could explain why Soto 2005 and Downing 2000 found guidance while Downing and Dodds 2004 and Woodman and Luck 2007 did not: memory load (1 item vs 2-3), articulatory suppression through the trial, and gap length (188 ms vs 1-2 s).
numbers: Gap 188 ms (Soto 2005, 2006b) vs 1 and 2 s (Woodman and Luck; Downing and Dodds). Load 1 item vs 2 or 3.
limits: Their own Exps 1-4 test these. The gap alone did not remove the effect (Exp 1).
agent_relevance: The effect is conditional, not universal. Treat held-lesson bias as a risk that depends on conditions.

source: Woodman and Luck (2007) Do the contents of visual working memory automatically influence attentional selection during visual search? Exp 1
finding: Failed to replicate automatic capture. One coloured square held; in search, one distractor matched its colour. No slowing from the match.
numbers: N=10. RT matching 1,475 vs mismatching 1,505 ms, F(1,9)=0.64, p>.40 (wrong direction for capture). Search accuracy 99.4% vs 98.9%. Memory accuracy 94.6% both.
limits: N=10. Matching vs mismatching only, no neutral baseline in Exps 1-3 (as read from PMC page; text beyond 100k characters not read). Long gap and suppression differ from Soto 2005.
agent_relevance: First clean null for automatic capture. Capture is not a law.

source: Woodman and Luck (2007) Exp 2: identical match in colour and gap
finding: Making the matching distractor identical to the held item (colour and gap) still gave no capture. The authors say with 95% confidence that any slowing was no more than 2.6 ms.
numbers: N=10. RT matching 1,455 vs mismatching 1,458 ms (difference -3.3 ms, 95% CI +/-5.9). F(1,9)=0.01. Memory accuracy 88.3% vs 90.0%.
limits: Same lab and N as Exp 1.
agent_relevance: A tight null bound. If capture exists it can be very small under these conditions.

source: Woodman and Luck (2007) Exp 3: three held items, matching distractor
finding: With three items held, a matching distractor made search faster, not slower. Observers seem to use held content as a template for rejection. The authors say memory can be a template for selection or for rejection, depending on the task.
numbers: N=10. RT matching 1,327 vs mismatching 1,394 ms (67 ms faster), F(1,9)=14.47, p<.01. Search error 0.2% vs 1.5%, p<.06. Memory accuracy 71% vs 68%.
limits: N=10. Load is confounded with the other changes, as Soto and Humphreys (2008) point out.
agent_relevance: Counter-result: if the agent knows an item is irrelevant, the held copy can be used to suppress it. Labelling a held lesson as a do-not-pick item may flip the sign.
quote: the contents of working memory can be used as either a template for selection or a template for rejection

source: Han and Kim (2009) Do the contents of working memory capture attention? Yes, but cognitive control matters
finding: Reconciles Soto 2005 and Woodman and Luck 2007. Capture by memory content appeared, but vanished when search was perceptually demanding or when search onset was delayed long enough for cognitive control to be set.
numbers: Numbers not read (abstract only).
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Two levers: make the search hard, and give time for control to set in. A pause before the search step may let control override the pull.

source: Olivers, Meijer, Theeuwes (2006) Feature-based memory-driven attentional capture
finding: Seven experiments. Singleton distractors interfered more when a memory task was added, and most when the distractor was identical or related to the held object, but only if the content was hard to verbalise. The effect held for memory-relevant features, not irrelevant features, and not for objects that could be forgotten. Memory-related distractors drew more eye movements but not longer fixations.
numbers: Seven experiments (details not read).
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: The pull is stronger for features held on purpose, and weaker for items marked as forgettable. A scaffold could mark a lesson as done and drop it from active context.

source: Soto and Humphreys (2009) Automatic selection of irrelevant object features through working memory
finding: Observers held only the shape of a coloured object. Search was impaired when a distractor matched both colour and shape of the cue. The abstract reports no impairment for a single-dimension match.
numbers: Numbers not read.
limits: Abstract only. This conflicts with Gao et al. 2016, where an irrelevant-feature match alone slowed search; task details differ.
agent_relevance: Pull may follow the whole bound object. A close paraphrase of a lesson may pull less than an exact repeat. Evidence is mixed.

source: Gao, Yu, Zhu, Shui, Weng, Li, Shen (2016) Object-based encoding in visual working memory: evidence from memory-driven attentional capture
finding: A task-irrelevant feature of a held object also captured attention. Search began 190 ms after the memory array. Distractors matching the relevant feature, the irrelevant feature, or both slowed search versus a neutral baseline.
numbers: N=22. Neutral 998 ms; irrelevant-match 1,036 (p=.001); relevant-match 1,065 (p<.001); conjunction 1,055 (p=.001). Relevant vs irrelevant p=.036. Exposure 100 ms: 1,074 vs 1000 ms: 1,003. No exposure x match interaction, F(3,63)=0.65, p=.59. Memory accuracy 95%; search accuracy 99%.
limits: RT only; errors at ceiling. Single lab.
agent_relevance: Features nobody asked to remember still pull. Incidental wording in a lesson may tilt what is noticed.

source: Carlisle, Arita, Pardo, Woodman (2011) Attentional templates in visual working memory
finding: Human electrophysiology for the template idea. The contralateral delay activity (CDA), a marker of working-memory load, was present when the target changed each trial, and faded over repeated same-target trials as long-term memory took over guiding search.
numbers: Exp 1 (N=20): CDA one target -0.8 uV, two targets -1.5 uV; CDA vs search speed r=-0.68 (p<.05). Exp 2 (N=10, same target throughout): no CDA, F<1. Exp 3 (N=18): CDA -0.66 (trials 1-2), -0.50 (3-4), -0.30 uV (5-7); interaction F(2,34)=3.83, p<.05; CDA vs RT r=0.90.
limits: Small N per experiment. Only 1 or 2 targets tested. P3 confound possible in the two-target contrast.
agent_relevance: Working-memory templates guide search only for roughly the first one to two trials after a target change; then long-term memory takes over. Fresh held content has the strongest pull right after it is loaded.

source: Olivers, Peters, Houtkamp, Roelfsema (2011) Different states in visual working memory: when it guides attention and when it does not
finding: Items in working memory differ in state. One item at a time holds the status of attentional template and drives attention. Other, accessory items do not bias attention.
numbers: No numbers (review).
limits: Abstract only. Offers a reading of Woodman and Luck 2007 (several items, no capture) versus Soto 2005 (one item, capture).
agent_relevance: Keep at most one active template in view for the step at hand. Park other lessons in a passive store.

source: Van der Stigchel and Olivers (2019) Attention is an emergent property of maintaining the task goal (reply to Oberauer)
finding: Argues that memory-driven bias arises for items serving the current task goal, through sensory recruitment. Memory not serving a current goal can be recoded to verbal labels or moved to long-term memory, and then stops biasing.
numbers: Cites van Moorselaar, Theeuwes, Olivers (2016) and Gayet et al. (2019): memory-induced bias drops across repeated memorising of the same item within one or two trials, though memory improves.
limits: Short commentary; no new data.
agent_relevance: Matches Carlisle 2011: a repeated lesson stops guiding via working memory. Bias returns when a new item is expected.

source: Sasin and Nieuwenstein (2016) Memory-driven capture reveals the waxing and waning of working memory activation due to dual-task interference
finding: Residual activation from judging a word (animacy) captured attention in a later RSVP stream, producing an attentional blink for the next target. An intervening arithmetic task erased this capture. When the word had to be remembered, capture survived the arithmetic task.
numbers: Exp 1a: 67 recruited, 9 excluded (N=58). No arithmetic: lag 2 accuracy 75.2% vs lag 7 81.9%, t(57)=3.22, p=.002, d=0.42. With arithmetic: 80.0% vs 80.1%, BF=6.96 for no difference. Interaction F(1,57)=4.30, p=.043. Exp 1b: 16 excluded; lag 2 75.8% vs lag 7 80.1%.
limits: Interaction only p=.043. Picture-from-word capture, not search with a distractor.
agent_relevance: Goal-held content survives interruption; merely processed content does not. An unrelated step can wash out leftover bias from earlier text, but not a deliberately kept lesson.

source: Soto, Hodsoll, Rotshtein, Humphreys (2008) Automatic guidance of attention from working memory
finding: Review of the field. Guidance from working memory occurs automatically, even when detrimental. Imaging data suggest the mechanism differs from bottom-up priming from implicit memory. Discusses early deployment of attention and gating into awareness.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Abstract only (full text paywalled).
agent_relevance: Held-content bias is distinct from simple repetition priming. A scaffold should not treat all repeated words as one effect.

source: De Fockert, Rees, Frith, Lavie (2001) The role of working memory in visual selective attention
finding: Load theory side of the conflict. High working-memory load (digits in new order each trial) increased interference from distractor faces and raised face-related activity in visual cortex. Working memory is needed to keep distractors out.
numbers: Numbers not read.
limits: Abstract only. The held digits did not match the distractor, so this is control loss, not content matching.
agent_relevance: Opposite sign to biased competition: more load means more distraction through weaker control. A heavy context may raise distraction even with no match.

source: Reynolds and Heeger (2009) The normalization model of attention
finding: Formal model: stimulus drive times an attention field, divided by a suppressive drive that pools neighbouring responses. It reproduces many attention effects and reconciles biased competition with feature-similarity gain accounts, depending on stimulus size and attention-field spread.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Abstract only. Neuron-level model.
agent_relevance: A concrete family: output = (drive x gain) / (pooled drive + constant). A template for a scoring rule that boosts items matching held content and divides by competing items.

source: Deco and Rolls (2005) Attention, short-term memory, and action selection: a unifying theory
finding: Spiking neural model where an attentional state held in prefrontal short-term memory biases ventral and dorsal stream areas through biased competition. It links the bias to action selection, and shows that absence of an expected reward can switch the bias.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Formal link between held content, bias and choice. A held bias can be reset when expected reward fails, which parallels our rule to revise on a failed check.

source: Deco and Rolls (2004) A neurodynamical cortical model of visual attention and invariant object recognition
finding: Hierarchical cortical model with top-down feedback from parietal or inferotemporal modules. Explains why attentional modulation grows from V1 to IT and why IT receptive fields shrink in cluttered scenes.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: The same bias mechanism acts at several levels, so one held item can tilt many later steps.

source: Hautekiet, Lewis-Peacock and colleagues (2026) Memory-driven attentional capture is not explained by inefficient task switching
finding: Two preregistered experiments: a held colour (reproduced at the end) and a search with a related or unrelated distractor. Capture replicated: slower with a related distractor. Cues to focus on the search, and an interruption task, did not convincingly remove it.
numbers: Numbers not read (preprint abstract only).
limits: Preprint; abstract only.
agent_relevance: Strong 2026 support that the pull is not just a failure to switch. A prompt that says to stop thinking about the lesson is unlikely to be enough.

source: Kim, Kwon, Heo, Han (2026) Conditional automaticity of memory-driven attention: dissociable effects on reaction time and accuracy
finding: Memory-matching distractors reliably slowed responses, but caused no extra accuracy loss beyond nonmatching distractors. The effect showed in time, not in report accuracy.
numbers: Two search tasks (T/L search and line search); numbers not read.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: The cost may be delay, not wrong answers. For an agent, held-lesson bias may cost steps more than correctness, which is cheaper to fix.

source: Liu, Wang, Liu (2026) The behavioral cost of memory-driven attentional capture: eye-movement evidence for post-capture processing
finding: Memory-matching distractors got more first fixations than neutral ones. If the distractor was not fixated, no extra search-time cost appeared. If fixated, dwell time grew. Higher working-memory capacity linked to less post-capture dwell, not to less initial capture.
numbers: Numbers not read.
limits: Preprint; abstract only.
agent_relevance: Two stages: capture, then processing cost. Disengagement after capture is where capacity helps, so a quick drop rule after a bad pick may matter more than preventing the pick.

source: Won and Zhang (2025) Search strategy modulates memory-driven capture
finding: A distractor matching the held colour captured strongly during feature search. During singleton-detection search (bottom-up mode) there was less capture. The internal search set changes the pull.
numbers: Two experiments; numbers not read.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Task framing changes how much held content tilts attention. The prompt that frames a step can raise or lower fixation.

source: Shi, Chen, Misra, Scales, Dohan, Chi, Scharli, Zhou (2023) Large language models can be easily distracted by irrelevant context
finding: GSM-IC: grade-school maths with one irrelevant sentence added. Accuracy fell sharply for all prompting methods. Distractors that overlapped with the problem (same role name) hurt most. Self-consistency, exemplars that include distractors, and an instruction to ignore irrelevant information each helped.
numbers: Of problems solved at baseline, no more than 18% were solved for every type of irrelevant sentence. Macro accuracy under 30% for most settings. text-davinci-003 macro accuracy 0 on role-overlap distractors with more than 2 steps. Self-consistency (20 samples): micro accuracy +11 points overall, +35.5 for 0-shot CoT; correct answer in the 20 samples for 99.7% (CoT, LTM); best macro accuracy only 45%. Distractor exemplars did not hurt original GSM8K.
limits: Older models (code-davinci-002, text-davinci-003). Distractors sit in the problem, not in held lessons. Maths only.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue to a matching distractor: overlap with the problem text raises the pull. Tested fixes: sampling plus a code-chosen vote, and demonstrating how to ignore. G4 warns that sample agreement is not proof, but recall within samples was near total.

source: Liu, Lin, Hewitt, Paranjape, Bevilacqua, Petroni, Liang (2023) Lost in the middle: how language models use long contexts
finding: Multi-document question answering: accuracy depends on where the relevant passage sits in the context. Best at the start or end, worst in the middle (U-shape). The U-shape appeared in sufficiently large Llama-2 models, with or without fine-tuning; instruction tuning did not remove it.
numbers: Closed-book accuracy: GPT-3.5-Turbo 56.1% (oracle 88.3%), Claude-1.3 48.3% (oracle 76.1%). More than 20 retrieved documents added only about 1.5 points (GPT-3.5-Turbo) and 1 point (Claude-1.3). Query before and after documents fixed key-value retrieval but not multi-document QA.
limits: 2023 models. Tests position of relevant text, not a matching distractor.
agent_relevance: Position in context is another bias on what the model notices. Put a key lesson at an edge of the prompt, not in the middle.

source: Niu, Yuan, Wang, Saghir, Abdi and colleagues (2025) Llama see, llama do: a mechanistic perspective on contextual entrainment and distraction in LLMs
finding: Language models give higher probability to any token that appeared earlier in the prompt, even random tokens. The size is larger for counterfactual than factual context. A small set of attention heads (entrainment heads) drives it. Setting those heads to zero sharply weakens the effect.
numbers: Shifts significant, p<0.0001 (paired t-tests), across relations in Llama-3.1-8B and other models. 36 entrainment heads found for the country-capital relation; across relations 3.2% to 10.7% of heads. Removing them has negligible to small effect on other abilities.
limits: Open-weights models; token probabilities on fact-recall prompts, not full problem solving.
agent_relevance: A mechanistic version of held-content pull: what is in context is tilted toward, relevant or not. The scaffold cannot switch heads off, but it can avoid placing wrong or counterfactual lesson text in context.

source: Gunseli, Fahrenfort, van Moorselaar, Daoultzis-Kontonis, Meeter, Olivers (2019) EEG dynamics reveal a dissociation between storage and selective attention within working memory
finding: Storage and selective attention within working memory are separate processes. With an unreliable retro-cue, cued items were attended but others stayed stored. Later, unattended items lost information even as attention moved back.
numbers: N=30. Recall error invalid 18.97 vs valid 12.92 degrees; validity x reliability F(1,29)=6.49, p=.016 (cue effect 8.27 deg at 80% valid vs 3.83 at 50% valid).
limits: Orientation recall; no distractor competition.
agent_relevance: Attending to an item and keeping it are different. A lesson can sit in context without steering attention, and steering can move without erasing it.
